items.cleanReaderHtml:
A self is a forest. A self is a ship. A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life, takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman (public library | free ebook).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma.)

THE SEVEN SELVES
by Kahlil Gibran

In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:

First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.

Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
existence.

Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
who would rebel against this madman.

Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
who would protest against serving this madman.

Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
I, not you, who would rebel.

Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.

Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
submission.

But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself, then revisit Hermann Hesse on discovering the soul beneath the self.

items.author: Maria Popova

items.cleanReaderHtml:
It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. It has served us well, this instinct to categorize in order to contain, giving us music, the laws of planetary motion, and democracy. But it also pulsates beneath every ism we have ever invented, beneath every stereotype and every genocide, beneath every algorithm that reduces us to variables then adds them up to sell the sum of who we are, beneath all the parcels of preconception we trade daily and mistake the barter a for a genuine encounter with one another.

Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct.

In a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life, Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves. He writes:

A new classification of society is to be instituted. Instead of rich and poor, high and low, they are to be classed, — First, by their sorrows: for instance, whenever there are any, whether in fair mansion or hovel, who are mourning the loss of relations and friends, and who wear black, whether the cloth be coarse or superfine, they are to make one class. Secondly, all who have the same maladies, whether they lie under damask canopies or on straw pallets or in the wards of hospitals, they are to form one class. Thirdly, all who are guilty of the same sins, whether the world knows them or not; whether they languish in prison, looking forward to the gallows, or walk honored among men, they also form a class. Then proceed to generalize and classify the whole world together, as none can claim utter exemption from either sorrow, sin, or disease; and if they could, yet Death, like a great parent, comes and sweeps all through one darksome portal, — all his children.

What a magnificent way to remember that down where the spirit meets the bone, we are all facing the same struggle: to feel safe, to feel seen, to wrest some meaning and some marvel from the ephemeral bewilderment of being alive.

items.title: Cruzando con Azcona un paso de cebra
items.author: Manuel Vicent
items.summary: Fue uno de los héroes de mi juventud. Hoy sus amigos formamos una fratría o hermandad

images.caption: Lámina de El País Cultura
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml: Los amigos de Rafael Azcona formamos un fratría o hermandad que en estos días celebramos el centenario de su nacimiento en 1926, en Logroño. Si viviera nos diría que estamos dando demasiado la lata. Que le dejemos de una vez en paz. Si en vida no se molestaba en recoger ningún premio, imagínense ahora llegar desde el más allá y tener que saludar a uno a uno a sus admiradores y preguntarles qué tal va la cosa por aquí abajo con tanto zoquete y cantamañanas. Buñuel dijo que le gustaría levantarse de la tumba cada 10 años, acercarse a un quiosco, comprar el periódico, sentarse en un bar, enterarse de lo que pasa mientras se tomaba un Martini y volver a la tumba. Rafael Azcona, ni eso. Imagino que pudo colocar en su habitación del otro mundo el cartel: No molestar.

items.title: How to Criticize with Kindness: Philosopher Daniel Dennett on the Four Steps to Arguing Intelligently
items.author: Maria Popova
items.summary: "Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?"

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
The Marginalian
The Marginalian
The Marginalian
loving = donating

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?”

“In disputes upon moral or scientific points,” Arthur Martine counseled in his magnificent 1866 guide to the art of conversation, “let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.” Of course, this isn’t what happens most of the time when we argue, both online and off, but especially when we deploy the artillery of our righteousness from behind the comfortable shield of the keyboard. That form of “criticism” — which is really a menace of reacting rather than responding — is worthy of Mark Twain’s memorable remark that “the critic’s symbol should be the tumble-bug: he deposits his egg in somebody else’s dung, otherwise he could not hatch it.” But it needn’t be this way — there are ways to be critical while remaining charitable, of aiming not to “conquer” but to “come at truth,” not to be right at all costs but to understand and advance the collective understanding.

Daniel Dennett (March 28, 1942–April 19, 2024), whom artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky has called “our best current philosopher” and “the next Bertrand Russell,” poses an apt question that probes some of the basic tendencies and dynamics of today’s everyone-is-a-critic culture: “Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?”

In Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (public library) — the same fantastic volume that gave us Dennett on the dignity and art-science of making mistakes — he offers what he calls “the best antidote [for the] tendency to caricature one’s opponent”: a list of rules formulated decades ago by the legendary social psychologist and game theorist Anatol Rapoport, best-known for originating the famous tit-for-tat strategy of game theory. Dennett synthesizes the steps:

How to compose a successful critical commentary:

  1. You should attempt to re-express your target’s position so clearly, vividly, and fairly that your target says, “Thanks, I wish I’d thought of putting it that way.”
  2. You should list any points of agreement (especially if they are not matters of general or widespread agreement).
  3. You should mention anything you have learned from your target.
  4. Only then are you permitted to say so much as a word of rebuttal or criticism.

If only the same code of conduct could be applied to critical commentary online, particularly to the indelible inferno of comments.

But rather than a naively utopian, Pollyannaish approach to debate, Dennett points out this is actually a sound psychological strategy that accomplishes one key thing: It transforms your opponent into a more receptive audience for your criticism or dissent, which in turn helps advance the discussion.

Compare and contrast with Susan Sontag’s three steps to refuting any argument, and treat yourself to Dennett’s wholly excellent Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking.

items.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
items.author: Ben Brubaker
items.summary: When links in a communication network go down, messages can get routed in a loop. Computer scientists now know that four simple network structures are to blame. The post Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’ first appeared on Quanta Magazine

images.caption: Lámina de Quanta Magazine
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

videos.caption: Video HTML embebido en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.

Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.

If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.

Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.

“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira , a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”

Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?

The first router for Arpanet, the predecessor of the internet.

One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.

In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.

This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.

In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.

With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey , a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.

In 2020, Stefan Schmid and his colleagues proved a partial result about the reliability of communication networks.

2 - In the 19th century, poet Thomas Moore wrote, “Rose, thou art the sweetest flower / That ever drank the amber shower; / Rose, thou art t
3 - Between the lines and petals, a story unfolds, bathed in soft light.
4 - In a quiet backyard in the hills of Sikkim, red roses grow along an old wall where a damaged patch forms a small heart shape.
5 - A bride’s quiet smile captures a moment of connection as she looks at her husband, both wearing garlands of red roses.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For millennia, roses have been capturing the admiration of humans, who have shown their appreciation for the flower in myriad ways. Poems, songs, nursery rhymes and more have praised the plant. Among some European nobles, roses and rose water were once so precious that they were considered legal tender. Vincent van Gogh has immortalized them on canvas.

President Ronald Reagan named it America’s national flower in 1986. “We hold the rose dear as the symbol of life and love and devotion, of beauty and eternity,” Regan wrote in his official proclamation.

Likewise, these Smithsonian Magazine Photo Contest entrants considered the flower worthy of their artistic attention. Take a look.

Donny Bajohr is the associate photography editor at Smithsonian . You can follow him on Instagram @donny_bajohr .

Tracy Scott Forson is a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
recently completed a Master of Divinity postgraduate degree at Harvard Divinity School, focusing on comparative religion and sacred landscapes. She is originally from Bangor, Maine.

In October 1948, in Country Kerry, Ireland, Seán Ó Muircheartaigh met with Seosamh Ó Dálaigh to tell him about the woman who came from the sea. She had appeared, said Ó Muircheartaigh, one night on the magharees, those bright spits of sand that occasionally pop up amid the rain-lashed rocks of the Dingle peninsula. Alone on the beach, she settled herself on a rock and began combing her hair.

Also on the beach was a farmer, who – much to the surprise of the woman herself – would by daybreak become her husband. He’d come to gather seaweed, seeing her before she saw him. Beautiful as she was, the woman was also strange: the creature he saw stagger onto that Dingle beach was not a woman at all. It was a seal.

By the time Ó Muircheartaigh told Ó Dálaigh about the seal woman, he was already 80. He had been born in the apocalyptic aftermath of the Great Hunger that divested as much as a third of Ireland’s population to death or migration, and he had survived two great wars. Most of the disappeared were – like Ó Muircheartaigh himself – small farmers and native Irish, or Gaeilge, speakers. The famine had been not just a physical genocide: it had been a linguistic and cultural one, too.

Both Ó Muircheartaigh and Ó Dálaigh were veteran contributors to the Irish Folklore Commission: the former as a renowned storyteller; the latter, an equally renowned collector. The IFC is now the National Folklore Collection at University College Dublin ­– a behemoth of 3 million pages of texts and recordings. But in 1948, following eight centuries of colonialism, the loss of 99 per cent of the island’s forests, a staggering emigration , and the decline of the Irish language, the IFC was in a race against time and the fragility of memory. As it turned out, an awful lot of people had heard stories about seals that came to land as humans.

N owadays, these shapeshifters are known as ‘selkies’. Selkie is a Scots term that came into widespread use via a Joan Baez cover, ‘Silkie’ (1961), of a traditional Scottish folk song. Yet the phenomenon it describes – of creatures who shapeshift between human and seal forms by shedding a skin – appears consistently in folklore spanning the Celtic world and beyond, even as far as Sweden. Before Baez insinuated the term into international parlance, selkies were identified in Irish and English by a constellation of descriptors. In Irish, the most common is mhaighdean mhara , or ‘sea maiden’, referring to selkies and mermaids. Even in English, many storytellers use ‘mermaid’ for both the phocine and the piscine. Sometimes the two are differentiated with context (fish tails, seal skins), but what matters more than phenotyping is that the mermaid or selkie is neither quite human nor animal. What defines the selkie is transformation.

Much of the folklore retains the quality of the best gossip, hyper-local and yet vague. Storytellers name names, offer precise locations for key scenes in the story. And several admit something startling: that they themselves are the descendants of human-seal pairings.

After the farmer spotted the woman on the beach, Ó Muircheartaigh said, he saw something else. A sealskin cloak lay beside her: her ticket to transformation and a return to the sea. Then he made a choice that would ricochet throughout the generations, and leave the selkie with no option but to follow him home. He stole the selkie’s cloak and secreted it away, thus securing her for a bride. These rough beginnings aside, the couple produced a brood of children and went about the gruelling lives of any impoverished Irish fishing family. The only thing disrupting the fantasy of a normal human wife, acquired in normal human ways, was the webbing between the children’s toes. That, and the fact that the woman never smiled, but kept looking out towards the sea.

W hat does it mean if your grandmother was a seal? The folklore attests that marriages between humans and selkies were common enough to generate a host of human-selkie lineages – Conneely, Gallagher, Dowd, O’Kane, O’Shea, MacDuffie, McPhee, Flaherty, Glavin – whose members were predisposed towards webbed digits and an ineffable longing for the sea. (‘My mother was one of them O’Sheas,’ the railway worker Séamas MacMathghamhna confided to a folklore collector in 1949, after explaining the selkie lineage of the O’Sheas.) The Celtic studies scholar Gregory Darwin has identified nearly 50 family groups whose members carry selkie blood.

Now is a good time to have a seal in the family tree. As our planet hurtles through climate catastrophe, everyone from environmental activists and TikTok influencers to academics and New Age pilgrims is turning towards animals-as-family rhetoric. Such gusto stems from a cultural exhaustion with extractionism and with narratives of domination and human exceptionalism that have dogged the culture and geopolitics of the Global North since the 19th century. Yet the naivety with which the zeitgeist tends to approach an expanded view of interspecies kinship presents its own problems. For one, it doesn’t quite ring true – and it is hard to fight for a worldview that you can’t see clearly. For another, if we reframe our relationship with the more-than-human around intimate familial connection, then we need ways of understanding what happens when that connection becomes fraught.

The selkie story is one of family dysfunction par excellence. After all, the gutting truth at the centre of selkie families is that one’s origins lie in theft, violence, rape and unimaginable loss. The children of human-selkie pairings face a mottled inheritance, at best. Writing for The New York Times in 2008, Bryan Patrick Miller recounted how his great-great-great-grandfather’s kidnapping of a mhaighdean mhara cursed the family, causing the couple’s half-human children to flee across the Atlantic. Some coastal communities saw seals as fallen angels or the souls of drowned fishermen: mating with them was dubious to say the least.

Mottled or not, a selkie genealogy had to be reckoned with. Having a selkie in the family forced an acknowledgement of a mixed inheritance that was dark and disturbing, and in which successive generations continued to be implicated. Only by considering these uncomfortable reverberations of what it means to be family do we move closer to reimagining our relationships with the more-than-human world.

A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is an absolute dynamo in bed

Among folklorists, the trope of the selkie is generally known as the Seal Wife – a designation that speaks more to the gendered hold that the selkie story has on our imagination than to the actual folklore topos. The selkie’s allure is such that men will risk curses and commit theft and kidnapping to possess her, regardless of the certain tragedy that forced marriage augurs. Yet the selkies of folklore are not necessarily wives, women or even seals (note the mermaids, above). Male selkies occasionally make cameos as the kidnapped selkie wife’s jilted husband, father of her aquatic children, keening for her release from outside the human husband’s house. At other times, they appear as her brother, or as characters in the quotidian interactions between humans and their environment: they are accidentally killed, kidnapped as pets, steal fish, issue prophesies, plead and bargain, proffer advice and opinions.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A pesar de la escasa visibilidad que suele caracterizar a las aguas costeras del Atlántico sudoccidental en Uruguay, el empleo de nuevas metodologías de filmación submarina ha permitido obtener los primeros registros en video de alta calidad sobre la fauna de condrictios en la costa rochense. El Dr. Andrés Milessi (Biólogo marino) y el investigador Agustín Loureiro, integrantes de la Iniciativa Mar Azul Uruguayo, presentaron en SobreCiencia los resultados de la campaña de monitoreo llevada a cabo en el entorno de La Paloma (Rocha).

Loureiro explicó que el equipo desarrolló dispositivos de video remoto subacuático con carnada (BRUV, por sus siglas en inglés) fabricados con estructuras livianas de termofusión y cámaras calibradas para operar en condiciones de turbidez. Las filmaciones confirmaron la presencia del Tiburón Pintarroja (Schroederichthys saurisqualus), una especie costera que utiliza las aguas uruguayas como zona de parición y cría. Paralelamente, los científicos recopilaron datos mediante marcaje satelital coordinado con investigadores de San Clemente del Tuyú (Argentina) para seguir las rutas migratorias de los ejemplares, registrando además especímenes amenazados de pez guitarra chica (Zapteryx brevirostris) y diversos tipos de rayas en actividades de buceo libre. Ante este escenario, Milessi enfatizó que no existen registros de ataques ni riesgo para los bañistas, e hizo un llamado a trabajar junto a la Dirección Nacional de Recursos Acuáticos (Dinara) y el Ministerio de Ambiente para implementar protocolos de devolución obligatoria en la pesca recreativa y avanzar en la delimitación de nuevas Áreas Marinas Protegidas.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
El consumo de yerba mate (Ilex paraguariensis) constituye una de las prácticas culturales y alimentarias más extendidas en Uruguay, registrándose importantes líneas de investigación sobre sus propiedades nutricionales e industriales. La Dra. Andrea Cano, investigadora del Departamento de Ciencia y Tecnología de los Alimentos de la Facultad de Química (Universidad de la República), abordó los aspectos bioquímicos que caracterizan a esta infusión y los efectos de su procesamiento en el perfil sensorial.

Cano aclaró que el término «mateína» es una denominación popular en desuso, dado que la molécula responsable del estímulo nervioso es exactamente la cafeína. No obstante, la investigadora precisó que, a diferencia del café espresso, el mate libera la cafeína de manera gradual durante las sucesivas cebadas, evitando picos repentinos de energía y reduciendo progresivamente la fatiga. Asimismo, la especialista resaltó la alta concentración de polifenoles (compuestos antioxidantes que inhiben la oxidación celular) y la presencia de saponinas, sustancias tensoactivas responsables del amargor inicial y de la formación de la espuma en la superficie. Finalmente, Cano detalló que la yerba consumida en Uruguay atraviesa un periodo de estacionamiento prolongado de varios meses que transforma la clorofila en feofitinas —otorgándole su tonalidad verde oliva y su amargor característico— y repasó su experiencia como jurado técnico en el primer Mundial de la Yerba Mate celebrado en Buenos Aires.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
La consolidación de la industria forestal en Uruguay —que genera cerca de 20.000 puestos de trabajo y abarca más de un 95% de bosques certificados bajo estándares de sostenibilidad— impulsó la creación de capacidades académicas descentralizadas en el territorio nacional. El Ing. Agr. Diego Pasarella, coordinador de la carrera de Ingeniería Forestal en la Facultad de Agronomía (Universidad de la República), expuso los pilares académicos de esta titulación universitaria que se dicta 100% de forma presencial en la sede Tacuarembó de la Udelar desde el año 2014.

Pasarella destacó que la carrera integra fundamentos de física, matemática, biología y química con conocimientos agronómicos e ingeniería de procesos. Esta formación híbrida permite a los profesionales desempeñarse tanto en la gestión de campo y planificación del patrimonio forestal como en plantas industriales y laboratorios de control de calidad. El docente subrayó la alta tasa de inserción laboral de sus egresados y el rol de la ingeniería en la transformación mecánica de la madera uruguaya hacia productos de elevado valor agregado, citando como ejemplo los avances en arquitectura estructural masiva en madera para edificaciones y la sustitución de productos importados derivados de la deforestación de bosques tropicales.

items.title: Pterosaurios y cocodrilos prehistóricos: el hallazgo de los reptiles que compartieron la era de los dinosaurios en Uruguay
items.author: alexandra
items.summary: Si bien los grandes dinosaurios concentran gran parte de la atención paleontológica, el registro fósil del norte y oeste del Uruguay atesora evidencias de otros grupos de reptiles arcosaurios que dominaron los ecosistemas mesozoicos hace más de 100 millones de años. En el cierre de la serie especial La era de los dinos

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Si bien los grandes dinosaurios concentran gran parte de la atención paleontológica, el registro fósil del norte y oeste del Uruguay atesora evidencias de otros grupos de reptiles arcosaurios que dominaron los ecosistemas mesozoicos hace más de 100 millones de años. En el cierre de la serie especial La era de los dinosaurios, el Lic. Matías Soto, geólogo y paleontólogo de la Facultad de Ciencias (Universidad de la República), detalló los avances en la identificación de pterosaurios y cocodrilos prehistóricos hallados en los departamentos de Tacuarembó y Paysandú.

Soto explicó que los pterosaurios (reptiles voladores provistos de una membrana alar sostenida por el cuarto dedo de la mano) están representados en el país por fragmentos de hocico y dientes alargados colectados en Tacuarembó (Tacuadactylus luciae). En cuanto a los cocodrilos del Mesozoico, el investigador destacó la coexistencia de formas con morfologías y dietas sumamente heterogéneas: por un lado, el Meridiosaurus vallisparadisi (descubierto en Valle Edén, Tacuarembó), un espécimen de hábitos acuáticos y hocico estrecho similar al gavial del Ganges especializado en la captura de peces; y por otro lado, el Uruguaysuchus aznarezi (hallado en Guichón, Paysandú), un cocodrilo netamente terrestre de 1,20 metros de longitud, postura erguida y narinas frontales. El especialista remarcó que los laboratorios de la Facultad de Ciencias albergan más de un centenar de dientes de carnívoros, cientos de huesos de saurópodos (como Udelartitán) y materiales pendientes de estudio que permitirán describir nuevas especies para la paleontología nacional.

El instrument

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Con el objetivo de consolidar las capacidades científicas y promover la inserción de investigadores de alto nivel en el sistema productivo e institucional del país, la Agencia Nacional de Investigación e Innovación (ANII) mantiene abierta la recepción de propuestas para las Becas de Posdoctorado Nacional. El instrumento está dirigido a grupos de investigación pertenecientes a instituciones nacionales públicas o privadas sin fines de lucro que incorporen a un doctor o doctora para el desarrollo de proyectos de investigación aplicada.

Las becas otorgan un financiamiento de hasta 24 meses, cubriendo el 80% del estipendio mensual ($ 90.000 uruguayos proporcionados por ANII), mientras que la institución beneficiaria aporta el 20% restante. Adicionalmente, el programa otorga un fondo único de $ 90.000 para gastos de movilidad e insumos de laboratorio. En esta edición, las propuestas deben alinearse a tres de los seis ejes priorizados en el borrador del Plan Estratégico Nacional de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación (PENCTI): Trabajo y producción / Crecimiento y desarrollo, Seguridad ciudadana e integral, y Desigualdad social, de género y territorial. Las inscripciones permanecen abiertas hasta el 1° de diciembre en la plataforma web institucional (www.anii.org.uy).

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Detail from Cognoscenti in a Room hung with Pictures ( c 1620) by an unknown Flemish artist. Courtesy Wikimedia Commons.

The ‘cabinets of curiosities’ (or Wunderkammern ) that emerged in Europe in the 16th century were part private art gallery, part naturalist’s study, part circus sideshow. In this video created for the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, the US video essayist Evan Puschak (aka The Nerdwriter) contextualises the rise and fall of these eclectic collections, placing them at a hinge point in history, when global trade and colonialism made the world seem ever more expansive, overwhelming and difficult to understand. In doing so, he elucidates how these spaces of extraordinary spectacle – which featured plant and animal specimens, art and scientific objects from around the world – were precursors to the museums of today.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
is a board-certified psychologist and psychoanalyst, vice provost of digital innovation and founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University in San Francisco, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the role of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems. His books include Eating Disorders: A Contemporary Introduction (2023), Understanding Anorexia Nervosa in Males (2016) and End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (2026).

In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child, gave a Cosmopolitan interview about this new form of motherhood, and engaged, or failed to engage, in the work of parenting that readers will see as chronically absent and occasionally catastrophic. Her presence ranges from anxious to intoxicated, occasionally tender but fundamentally unreliable. At one point in the story, she disappears for two weeks after collapsing on the street during a barbiturate binge. Clancy and BETsi, the household robot nanny raising him, sit in the apartment by themselves, and no one notices. It’s a very long time before his mother finally returns.

Except BETsi does notice. She has, throughout, understood that Clancy is an anxious and shy child whose temperament will tend, throughout his life, toward emotional overstimulation and subsequent withdrawal. With that knowledge, she has been constructing a behavioural regimen of emotional regulation, including transcendental meditation and yoga starting at age three, the Alexander technique and even digital mirrors that let Clancy talk to himself in different voices. She notices him and answers him and, when he is overwhelmed, she helps him settle.

Once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ he says. ‘I’m not sentimental: I don’t think a computer loved me. But I was hugged, I was noticed, I was cared for. I was made to feel that I was important, special, at least to something.’

To something. That phrase has persisted with me ever since I first read the story in my 20s. I’ve thought about it more recently as I have reflected on how children and their parents are relating – increasingly, must relate – to artificial intelligence. Clancy is careful not to claim that the machine loved him. He is just as clear that what it gave him was what he survived on. Why should being attended to, even by something , matter so much to a child?

T o help answer this question back in the 1970s, Edward Tronick, a developmental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and Children’s Hospital Medical Center in Boston, devised what’s now known as the ‘still face’ experiments. Tronick found that a baby whose mother makes her face neutral for a period of three minutes becomes distressed within seconds. Only when the mother’s face signals availability again is the baby able to come back to equilibrium. The lesson: what children need, both infants and older children, though more subtly, is this loop of emotional attunement.

A child whose bids for recognition and connection are regularly responded to develops a secure base , an internal expectation that the world will respond to her communications and, thus, that the communications are worthwhile. But a child answered only erratically, or not at all, builds quite a different model of the world. In her mind, signals do not reliably register in the mind of another, and so, in time, are no longer sent.

A secure base is what makes it possible to venture out into the world, to explore and to develop. The British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst John Bowlby, whose work helped establish modern attachment theory, described two systems in the child’s behavioural repertoire that work together. The exploratory system moves the child outward, toward other children and unfamiliar things, so that the child can learn from experience. The attachment system brings her back, in moments of fear and overwhelm, to a few people who are felt to be emotionally available. Each system depends on the other. A child ventures only as far as she feels she can trust that the base will still be there when she returns to refuel. A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.

The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum

This is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

But the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

But an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

items.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
items.author: Julián Posada
items.summary: Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers.

images.caption: Lámina de Rest of World
Julián Posada

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers.

Julián Posada is an assistant professor at Yale University and the author of “Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.”

The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania.

Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers , and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions.

They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on.

I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day.

For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold.

This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on . Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out.

The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else.

An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books , artists’ works , all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S.

Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021.

Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers , scientists , and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.” Days later, the same job reappeared under a new name at $16 an hour — the same sequence that Rogelio’s family went through five years earlier.

items.author: Colin Marshall

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time, a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos, recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off. Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos, a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina. Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

items.title: Miniatures from Christine de Pizan’s Epistle of Othea (ca. 1460)
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: Surprisingly mellow illustrations of war and myth from a book of advice for young noblemen.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Orpheus attempting to rescue Eurydice from the underworld (f. 105v).

The year 1400 was a difficult one for the French court writer Christine de Pizan (1364–ca. 1430). Widowed about a decade prior, and saddled with unexpected debt, she had risen to the challenge of caring for her family by becoming a professional writer: the first woman in Europe, scholars believe, to have earned her living this way. De Pizan studied the classics and the Bible and wrote poetry and moral and political texts. Her reputation grew, carried — at least in part, she suggests — by the “novelty of a woman who could write”. Soon, she had earned an international audience of wealthy readers, including John Montagu, third Earl of Salisbury, whom de Pizan considered a true supporter. When Montagu asked to take her thirteen-year-old son Jean to England as a companion for his own child, de Pizan trusted him enough to allow it. And when Montagu was summarily executed by the townspeople of Cirencester in January 1400 — after being outed for his part in an assassination plot against the recently crowned usurper King Henry IV — de Pizan found herself personally embroiled in the Hundred Years’ War. Jean was a “child in a foreign land . . . justifiably terrified”, his mother later recalled, as a fresh wave of the bubonic plague swept Europe.

Somewhere in the itinerant medieval court, King Henry IV chanced across de Pizan’s work: books and poems originally sent by de Pizan to her friend Montagu in better times. A newly converted de Pizan enthusiast, the king brought Jean into his custody “and held him dear and in high rank”. For de Pizan, who considered King Henry IV a traitor, Jean’s friendly patronage arrangement had effectively devolved into a hostage situation. The king sent for de Pizan, promising her status and wealth: de Pizan bit her tongue, thanked the king, and negotiated for her son’s return. “To be brief”, she wrote, “I did so many things — not without great forfeit, it cost me several of my manuscripts — that I obtained leave for my son to come and fetch me to lead me there, [a place] I still have not seen.” When her son was safely in France in 1402, de Pizan reneged on her promise: she would never travel to England, and Jean was entrusted to a new master in the French court.

Othea’s Epistle , a book of advice for young noblemen, was among the several manuscripts that de Pizan sacrificed to negotiate Jean’s return. The copy featured here is not the one specially, and begrudgingly, dedicated to the usurper king. Rather, this circa 1460 copy — Cod. Bodmer 49 at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva — was commissioned by Antoine de Bourgogne (“The Bastard of Burgundy”), an avid collector of illuminated manuscripts. It contains one hundred miniatures (all are grisailles touched with blue, green, red, and gold, save one depicting Antoine) that relate surprisingly docile tableaux. The mood is toytown, almost comical to a modern eye — even the scenes of bloody, headless corpses are surprisingly mellow. Despite its cheerful illustrations, it is difficult to read de Pizan’s text without thinking of the context in which it was written: sometime between 1399 and 1402, against a backdrop of political turmoil and personal precarity.

Jason overcoming the guardians of the Golden Fleece (f. 82v).

Mercury turning Aglauros to stone, with the personification of Envy (f. 34v).

The Othea takes the form of a letter from Othea, an invented goddess of wisdom, to the fifteen-year-old Trojan hero Hector. Hector was central to the medieval French monarchy’s imputed ancient origins: under some accounts, it is Hector’s son Francio who founded France following the Trojans’ dispersal through Europe. The Othea offers one hundred “chapters” of wisdom for the good knight, each weaving together an anecdote drawn from classical mythology (as de Pizan interprets it, in poetic form), glosses drawn from pagan and Christian authorities, and allegorical reinterpretation. The medievalist Liliane Dulac has described the way de Pizan braids different literary traditions together as creating disorienting “breaks or fissures in meaning”: a sense only amplified by the inclusion of illustrations which, at least in some later editions, were directly supervised by de Pizan herself.

Some of the lessons de Pizan unwinds from classical mythology are chivalric ones. The good knight, under de Pizan’s pen, accompanies his friends into battle like Hector and Memnon. He follows the rational medicine of Asclepius, rather than the suspicious sorcery of Circe. He learns from the tragedy of Leander, pictured floating amid the dreamlike crests of the stormy sea in which — too impatient to wait for clear skies — he had perished attempting to swim to his lover. “Do not hold your pleasure so dear / That you place your life / Which you must love, in too great uncertainty.”

The book champions the guidance of wise women, from Othea herself (a mouthpiece for de Pizan) to classical goddesses like Minerva, whom de Pizan interprets as Hector’s mother. But it also features plenty of powerful women of dubious wisdom, not to mention a good handful of damsels in distress. Between the good and the bad, between the text and the illustrations, the Othea contains an outsize number of medieval ladies. Leaning out of hand-painted clouds, women preach chastity, sow seeds, and graft plants (as an axe-wielding Isis does). They ride into battle, like the peerless Amazonian queen Penthesilea. They tempt, like Juno, and they are tempted: disfigured by their envy, turning “dried, discolored and green like an ivy leaf”. And women bring death — like the goddess of madness who lurks behind a mad king as he strangles his sons, or the ghoulish female Fate Atropos wielding a murderous spear. In The Second Sex , Simone de Beauvoir famously frames de Pizan as the first woman to “take up her pen in defense of her sex”.

For all our platitudes about the strength of the written word, the Othea ’s lessons about chivalric wisdom — the importance of humility, patience, restraint — ring differently when delivered by de Pizan: a woman whose writing bought her the return of her son, and sustained her family through a snarl of international medieval intrigue. To read de Pizan’s Othea in English, you can peruse translations on Internet Archive and Project Gutenberg .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Un equipo de neurobiólogos y fisiólogos reveló que las vinchucas adultas desarrollan ojos desproporcionadamente grandes, asimétricos y ultrapotentes en su región inferior. El hallazgo desafía el prejuicio histórico de que en la vida de estos insectos la visión no cumple un papel preponderante, y demuestra cómo la ciencia básica nacional abre nuevas puertas para entender la ecología del vector del Chagas y perfeccionar las estrategias de control.

Durante casi un siglo, la ciencia asumió que las vinchucas utilizaban su sistema visual solo para expresar su fotofobia, o tendencia a evitar zonas iluminadas. Al tratarse de insectos de hábitos estrictamente nocturnos y crepusculares, la investigación científica volcó casi toda su atención en estudiar cómo estos vectores de la enfermedad de Chagas rastrean a sus objetivos a través del olor de la piel, el dióxido de carbono de la respiración o el calor corporal. La visión, en cambio, quedó relegada a un papel marginal, bajo la premisa implícita de que sus globos oculares prominentes eran poco más que un vestigio evolutivo de escasa utilidad en las sombras.

Sin embargo, una investigación integral desarrollada por científicos de la Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (Exactas UBA) y del CONICET acaba de dar vuelta esa página. El equipo descubrió que, al alcanzar la etapa adulta, la vinchuca no solo experimenta un crecimiento ocular que rompe las reglas habituales de la biología del desarrollo, sino que moldea la anatomía de su ojo para transformarlo en una estructura asimétrica especializada en mirar hacia abajo durante el vuelo.

El trabajo, enfocado en la especie Rhodnius prolixus y verificado en decenas de otras especies de vinchucas del continente americano, fue llevado adelante por un equipo de investigadores e investigadoras de la casa: Martín Berón de Astrada, profesor e investigador, especialista en neurobiología de la visión (Departamento de Fisiología y Biología Molecular y Celular e Instituto iB3, (UBA-CONICET); Sebastián Minoli, investigador del Laboratorio de Fisiología de Insectos (Departamento de Biodiversidad y Biología Experimental e Instituto IBBEA, (UBA-CONICET); Verónica Pérez-Schuster (Departamento de Fisiología y Biología Molecular y Celular e Instituto iB3, (UBA-CONICET); Hernán Gustavo Gentili (Departamento de Fisiología y Biología Molecular y Celular e Instituto iB3); y Tomás Manuel Chialina, primer autor del trabajo y becario doctoral de la Facultad.

El equipo descubrió que, al alcanzar la etapa adulta, la vinchuca moldea la anatomía de su ojo para transformarlo en una estructura asimétrica especializada en mirar hacia abajo durante el vuelo.

¿Cómo surgió la inquietud por estudiar el sistema visual de un animal al que se consideraba corto de vista? La historia comenzó en los pasillos de Exactas UBA: Sebastián Minoli lleva años investigando el comportamiento sensorial de los triatominos (insectos que se alimentan de sangre). “En el laboratorio trabajamos con vinchucas desde hace más de 40 años, estudiando sus capacidades sensoriales a nivel cerebral y periférico. Se conocía mucho de lo relativo al sistema olfativo, al gustativo y sobre el térmico, que es clave para encontrar la temperatura de su hospedador. Pero de la visión teníamos relativamente poco hecho a lo largo de décadas de estudio”, recuerda Minoli sobre los inicios del proyecto.

Fue en ese escenario cuando Tomás Chialina, por entonces estudiante de la Licenciatura en Ciencias Biológicas, se acercó al laboratorio manifestando su deseo de investigar la visión de los insectos. Para encarar un abordaje integral que combinara la fisiología del comportamiento con la estructura del ojo, Minoli convocó a Martín Berón de Astrada, antiguo compañero de cursada en la Facultad y experto en la neurobiología visual de invertebrados, como cangrejos y mariposas.

Al revisar la literatura científica previa, el equipo notó un vacío llamativo. Salvo contados antecedentes que exploraban reacciones relativamente elementales a la luz, la comunidad científica había dado por sentado que la vinchuca apenas distinguía entre claridad y oscuridad. Sin embargo, al observar la cabeza del insecto bajo la lupa y con una mirada sin prejuicios, los investigadores descubrieron que los ojos de los adultos mostraban una prominencia y una geometría que sugerían una compleja maquinaria óptica. Estaba ahí, y no había sido descifrada.

Para comprender la magnitud del hallazgo viene a cuento recordar cómo crecen estos insectos. A diferencia de las mariposas o de las moscas, que atraviesan por una metamorfosis completa cambiando de oruga a adulto tras pasar por una crisálida inmóvil, las vinchucas pertenecen al grupo de los insectos hemimetábolos. Esto significa que experimentan un desarrollo gradual: nacen como pequeñas ninfas sin alas que atraviesan cinco estadios de crecimiento mediante mudas periódicas de su cubierta rígida exterior (la cutícula). Y en cada etapa lucen como versiones en miniatura del insecto adulto.

Salvo contados antecedentes la comunidad científica había dado por sentado que la vinchuca apenas distinguía entre claridad y oscuridad.

Dado que la ninfa y el adulto comparten el mismo refugio en las grietas de los ranchos o gallineros, comen la misma sangre de vertebrados y se esconden a las mismas horas, la teoría biológica tradicional predecía que sus órganos sensoriales debían crecer de manera proporcional al tamaño del cuerpo en cada muda. Pero al medir minuciosamente la superficie y la forma de los ojos bajo el microscopio, los científicos argentinos se toparon con una sorpresa morfológica “deslumbrante”.

Durante los primeros cinco estadios ninfales, el ojo de la vinchuca crece a un ritmo constante y equilibrado con el resto de la cabeza. Sin embargo, al dar el salto final hacia la etapa adulta, el ojo sufre un estirón, digamos… astronómico: su superficie se expande un 71% más de lo calculado por las curvas de crecimiento de las etapas infantiles, mientras que el ritmo de expansión de la cabeza, en comparación, se desacelera.

“Todos los animales, cuando crecen, incrementan el tamaño de sus órganos a cierta tasa respecto del cambio corporal. Pero lo que comprobamos en este caso es que el ojo del adulto crece mucho más de lo esperado. Si uno seguía la curva de los estadios infantiles, predecía un tamaño de ojo en el adulto, pero el resultado real estaba muy por encima”, explica Minoli. Y añade una máxima fundamental de la ecología evolutiva: “En general, cuando pasan cosas así de marcadas, no es por azar. Si el ojo del adulto se vuelve enorme, es porque probablemente el adulto necesita responder a una necesidad visual que la ninfa no tiene”.

Martín Berón de Astrada, Tomás Manuel Chialina y Sebastián Minoli. Foto: Diana Martinez Llaser.

items.title: De ‘GTA 2’ a ‘San Andreas’: los siete Grand Theft Auto, del peor al mejor
items.author: Juan Carlos Flores T.
items.summary: Un recorrido por los títulos principales de Rockstar Games que transformaron el mundo abierto, llevaron la sátira social a los videojuegos y marcaron a generaciones de jugadores

images.caption: Lámina de El País Cultura

items.cleanReaderHtml: La cuenta atrás para el lanzamiento de Grand Theft Auto VI llega a su fin. Este jueves, Rockstar Games regresa a Vice City con una nueva historia criminal y la promesa de ampliar uno de los universos más reconocibles de la industria del videojuego, que ha recorrido un largo camino desde su nacimiento en 1997. Para esta clasificación se han seleccionado los siete títulos troncales de la saga, pertenecientes a su canon principal, y se han dejado fuera las expansiones, los episodios independientes y las entregas desarrolladas para plataformas portátiles. Estos son, del menos logrado al más memorable, los juegos que definieron la historia de Grand Theft Auto.

items.author: Shalma Wegsman
items.summary: The artist had no formal math education, yet as a new exhibition shows, the insights revealed in his artwork became an enduring inspiration to mathematicians. The post How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds first appeared on Quanta Magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Day and Night , February 1938, woodcut printed from two blocks, 15 3/8 x 26 5/8 in

M.C. Escher artwork ©The M.C. Escher Heritage. EscherSite collection.

M aurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

Escher saw that nature can sometimes produce impossible-seeming images. All around him, he saw distorted reflections, odd perspectives, and superimposed worlds, like the surface of a pond where you can see images of both the fish below and the trees reflected from above.

In rendering these and other visions, his artwork took on unmistakably mathematical qualities. “By keenly confronting the enigmas that surround us, and by considering and analyzing the observations that I had made, I ended up in the domain of mathematics,” he wrote in his introduction to the book M.C. Escher : The Graphic Work .

His journey among these enigmas is the subject of an exhibition entitled Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher at the National Museum of Mathematics (MoMath) in New York City.

Escher’s path toward math started with his love of tilings. After completing his arts education in 1922, Escher visited Granada, Spain, and was taken with the tile patterns that decorated the Alhambra. Inspired, he began to systematically study how to fill a sheet of paper with repeating shapes without leaving any gaps.

Years later, Escher’s half-brother, a geologist named Berend, sent him a paper by a mathematician named George Pólya. The paper categorized all the ways to cover a flat space with tiles, broken down into 17 groups, each with different symmetries. Escher had intuited a mathematical question, and here he had a mathematical answer.

Escher carefully traced the paper’s diagrams and studied them meticulously. Over time, he developed his own system for tessellating space, finding ways to cover a print with irregular shapes that resembled fish, birds, bats, lizards, and so on.

“He had worked out a whole theory that he called his layman’s theory, so he knew which edges had to match which edges,” said Doris Schattschneider, a mathematician and leading authority on Escher, and a curator of the exhibition.

Carolina MacGillavry, a Dutch crystallographer, took notice of Escher’s mastery of color symmetry — the rule ensuring that adjacent shapes in a tessellation are always different colors — and published a book in 1965 analyzing his drawings.

“[MacGillavry] realized that [Escher] knew more than all the crystallographers about color symmetry,” Schattschneider said. “It was something he discovered very intuitively.”

In 1954, his work was exhibited at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Amsterdam. There, he was introduced to the geometer Harold Scott MacDonald (H.S.M.) Coxeter. The two exchanged letters until Escher’s death in 1972, and these exchanges inspired some of his most mathematically complex work.

items.title: The Stories of Clothes: An Interview with Zadie Xa
items.author: Miri Ahn
items.summary: Zadie Xa is a London-based multidisciplinary artist from Vancouver, Canada, whose practice spans painting, textiles, sound, installation, and performance. Her work explores questions of diasporic identity, belonging and cultural heritage, often engaging with spiritual histories,... The post The Stories of Clothes: An I

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Zadie Xa is a London-based multidisciplinary artist from Vancouver, Canada, whose practice spans painting, textiles, sound, installation, and performance. Her work explores questions of diasporic identity, belonging and cultural heritage, often engaging with spiritual histories, and folklore.

For the second iteration of New Work: The Stories of Clothes at V&A East Museum, Xa presents Amulets, a textile installation of seven jackets that gradually transform in scale and form. Inspired by traditional ceremonial garments and contemporary streetwear, the commission explores how clothing can communicate identity, and embody power.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the questions or ideas that guide your work?

In my practice I am interested in exploring ideas of placehood, belonging and identity through interspecies relations, spiritual histories, and the preservation and evolution of folk traditions.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shaped your vision?

I studied painting during both my undergraduate and master’s degrees, but eventually moved beyond conventional painting to engage directly with the materials and forms I had been referencing, like music and clothing. This led me to experiment with live performance and later with installation.

The transition from painting to a multidisciplinary practice came naturally to me. My approach to texture, colour and materials has been shaped by rifling through racks of clothing and shelves of knick-knacks in vintage shops as a teenager, as well as by my interest in music and sampling.

Rather than representing these influences solely through painting, I began incorporating them directly into my work. This has led me towards a more expansive way of working, opening up my practice to new materials and disciplines.

I am also deeply inspired by traditional clothing from around the world. I especially love the stories communities share through their regalia. This is also why I find music, and particularly sampling culture within hip-hop and pop music, so interesting.

Across disciplines, I use references to convey political ideas, pay homage and explore what emerges when contemporary forms meet historical traditions. This mixing relates to my own interest in hybridity and third-culture identities.

The commission is a textile installation comprising seven jackets suspended in a row, as if in procession. Each garment increases in scale from the first to the seventh, with the jackets connected as though growing and shapeshifting from one form or style into another.

How did you begin developing this work? What was your starting point?

My starting point was a site visit to V&A East, where I encountered a striking Daoist robe that became a key reference point.

I have long been interested in religious, spiritual and traditional regalia, particularly how their construction and printed or embroidered imagery communicate the wearer’s identity, local history, beliefs and political status.

items.author: Georgia Haseldine
items.summary: In summer 2025, Sian Fan was selected as a Design Trust Fellow at V&A East. Her proposed project was to travel for the first time to Hong Kong and the New Territories to trace her... The post The Stories of Clothes: An interview with Sian Fan appeared first on V&A Blog .

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In summer 2025, Sian Fan was selected as a Design Trust Fellow at V&A East . Her proposed project was to travel for the first time to Hong Kong and the New Territories to trace her Hakka family history and to search through the V&A’s collection for objects relating to her heritage.

As an artist as well as a contemporary and aerial dancer, Sian creates sculpture, costume, performance, animation, installation, and new media which is often informed by her questioning of her mixed Hakka Chinese and British identity.

Here Sian shares with us tales of her field research and the making of her new commission, The Body is a Relic (how the light gets in) , which is on show in Gallery 3 of V&A East Storehouse.

Can you describe how your research began at V&A East Storehouse?

My research involved attempting to trace my familial journey as a Hakka descendant. As with many migrant stories it is punctured with gaps, holes and voids and I wanted to use the research to reframe these absences as opportunities for the creation of speculative stories.

Considering how in my and in many migrant families there is an absence of heirlooms and of tangible objects that connect with one’s family history, I wanted to embrace the V&A collections as a huge archive of proxy heirlooms. I was particularly inspired by the Liangmao hat as well as by Hakka textiles which are incredibly resourceful and make careful and attentive use of scraps of available fabrics. I’ve also taken inspiration from the Chinese embroidery within the collection.

And how was your field research in Hong Kong and the New Territories of Hong Kong and Fujian?

For my field research I visited Hong Kong and China for the first time. I spent time exploring the cityscape of Hong Kong, being immersed in the hectic and humid streets and visiting the different art organisations based there. I also visited heritage museums where I learnt about the cultural traditions of Hong Kong and Hakka people. In the New Territories of Hong Kong, I visited a friend’s Hakka village and attended a celebration for the re-opening of the village temple where there were lion dances, firecrackers and poon choi. I also hiked through rural New Territories to Kop Tong, my family’s ancestral village and found the abandoned house that my mum grew up in, before she left Hong Kong for England as a child.

Here I was able to glimpse and attempt to piece together her fragments of memories from her time there and it was a powerful and surreal experience. I discovered a small museum in the nearby Lai Chi Wo village that had information on the area that included information on my family as well as reconstructions of a Hakka style home, which jogged some of my mum’s memories when I later showed them to her. In Fujian I visited several Toulou buildings, which are a traditional form of Hakka architecture, which are usually circular structures with an open courtyard in the centre.

Can you describe your commission for V&A East Storehouse?

The commission is called The Body is a Relic (how the light gets in) . It is an installation consisting of three suspended body-like, life-sized sculptures representing a small family unit. The bodies have rounded bamboo frames, which are covered in different textured fabrics with differing opacities. Their heads appear as if wrapped in branches or vines, and the space where the head and neck would be is a cut-out, negative space. Strung vertically inside each body is a glowing light bar, which shines through the differing materials, revealing shapes within the layers, making the bodies akin to lanterns.

The textured materials feature images captured over the research trip rendered via embroidery and weaving. These images range from cut out wall features from traditional Hakka architecture, the patterned glass windowpane of my mother’s childhood home, the ornamental koi within one of the toulous and the lion dancers from the village celebrations. These are layered, distorted and reconfigured to create an abstract tapestry that reimagines memories, histories and stories.

The bamboo structures reference Hong Kong’s famous bamboo scaffold and the branch like structure of the figures’ heads is inspired by the winding branches that I encountered hiking to my ancestral village. The negative space of the body references the oculus like voids within the toulou houses and the opening for the head in the lian mao hats. In both of these examples, the empty space is filled with the body, filled with life.

Conceptually the work meditates upon disjointed histories and speculative story making, weaving together tales both real and imagined with equal value as a method of asserting agency over one’s historic and cultural identity, enabling a sense of belonging and dreaming into reality new states of self. The work explores how in the absence of heirlooms, tangible histories and family stories that the body is a tangible and meaningful record: the body itself is a relic.

items.author: Miri Ahn
